summary: Describes NFS version 4 minor version 1, including features kept from the base protocol and extensions, such as parallel NFS. It was replaced by RFC 8881.

plainLanguage.summary: NFS lets computers share files over a network as if on one disk. This is a newer version with extra features.

questions: what is a delegation in nfs
subtitle: NFS version 4.1: file sharing rebuilt around sessions, exactly-once requests and parallel access to storage.

tldr.problem: NFSv4.0 had no reliable way to avoid running a request twice after a retry, handled callbacks poorly through firewalls, could not use several network paths at once, and could not spread file data over many servers.
tldr.mechanism: NFSv4.1 adds a mandatory session layer, where every request carries a SEQUENCE operation with a slot and sequence number, plus directory delegations and parallel NFS (pNFS), which hands clients layouts so they can read and write storage devices directly.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5661 has been obsoleted by RFC 8881 and was updated by RFC 8178 and RFC 8434. The abstract calls minor version 1 superior to minor version 0 and says its use is preferred.

today: RFC 5661 is obsolete: RFC 8881 replaces it, and the RFC had been updated by RFC 8178 and RFC 8434. Its status was Proposed Standard, published in January 2010.

sections.title: What NFSv4.1 Adds
sections.content:
The Network File System (NFS) version 4 minor version 1 is the second minor version of NFSv4. It is a separate protocol with no dependencies on NFSv4.0 (RFC 3530), and the document neither updates nor obsoletes that RFC. Both minor versions can run at the same time between the same client and server.

The major extensions are sessions, directory delegations and parallel NFS (pNFS). Section 1.8 also lists the RECLAIM_COMPLETE operation, attributes set atomically during exclusive create with the new EXCLUSIVE4_1 method, open files preserved after their last link is removed, better compatibility with Windows access control lists, data retention attributes, identification of client and server implementations, and notification when a byte-range lock may be available.

NFSv4.1 breaks two of the NFSv4.0 minor-versioning guidelines. A server that supports minor version 1 does not have to support minor version 0, and a new feature, sessions, is mandatory. The authors say that making sessions and RECLAIM_COMPLETE anything but REQUIRED would add undue complexity.

The RFC is about 600 pages. This explainer follows its main structure: the RPC foundation, sessions, state and leases, caching with delegations, the namespace, and pNFS.
sections.plainLanguage: NFS is a way to use files that live on another computer. This new version fixes problems with the old one and adds ways to go faster.

sections.title: COMPOUND: Many Operations in One Request
sections.content:
NFSv4.1 is a Remote Procedure Call (RPC) application that uses RPC version 2 and the External Data Representation (XDR). In every NFSv4 minor version there are exactly two RPC procedures, NULL and COMPOUND. A COMPOUND is a series of individual operations, such as LOOKUP, GETATTR, OPEN and READ, that do the work of the traditional NFS procedures.

The server evaluates the operations in order, without any atomicity guarantee. When one fails, evaluation stops and the results of everything evaluated so far go back to the client. A client can chain several LOOKUP operations for a multi-component path, or combine OPEN with READ, to avoid extra round trips.

Unlike NFSv3, which used ancillary protocols such as NLM, NSM and MOUNT, all NFSv4 minor versions use a single RPC protocol. Locking is integrated, and the work of MOUNT is done by LOOKUP from a per-server global root filehandle.

The server can also call the client. There are two callback procedures, CB_NULL and CB_COMPOUND, built the same way. New operations can be added inside COMPOUND, which is how minor versions extend the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of sending one tiny note at a time, you hand over a whole to-do list, and the server works down the list until something goes wrong.

sections.title: RPC Security and Kerberos
sections.content:
Older NFS relied on host-based trust: the server trusted the client machine to vouch for its users, and AUTH_SYS carried only a user identity. NFSv4.1 clients and servers MUST implement RPCSEC_GSS, which uses GSS-API to give per-RPC authentication, integrity checking and, optionally, privacy. Implementing is required; using is not, so AUTH_SYS may still be used but is only an OPTIONAL flavor, and interoperability through it is not assured.

Both sides MUST support the integrity and authentication services. Servers MUST support the privacy service and clients SHOULD. Both MUST support the Kerberos V5 mechanism, with a QOP of zero so that the mechanism decides the protection level. The server identifies itself with a host-based service name of the form service@hostname, where the service is nfs; for Kerberos the form nfs/hostname is RECOMMENDED.

The RFC does not name required Kerberos algorithms. It says implementors should track the Kerberos standard, and that real security depends on the existing Kerberos infrastructure. It notes that AES with HMAC-SHA1 was REQUIRED at the time, whereas NFSv4.0 had to require weaker sets.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of trusting the building's front door, every single message is checked like a signed note, so the server knows who really sent it.

sections.title: Sessions, Channels and Connections
sections.content:
Sessions fix four NFSv4.0 shortcomings: no exactly once semantics, limited callback support (no callbacks through firewalls, and races between replies and callbacks), limited trunking over multiple network paths, and a need for machine credentials for full security. NFSv4.1 clients and servers MUST support and MUST use sessions.

A session is a long-lived server object that a client creates and uses from one or more transport connections. A single client may create several sessions, but a single session MUST NOT serve more than one client. State such as locks, delegations and layouts is tied to the client ID (a 64-bit identifier), not to any session, so a callback can arrive on a different session from the one that acquired the state. Any use of a session renews the client's lease.

Each session has a fore channel for client requests (COMPOUND) and may have a backchannel for server callbacks (CB_COMPOUND). The client creates the connections and gives them to the server, which solves the firewall problem. A connection can carry one channel or both, and the client can attach any number of connections, which gives trunking.

Setup runs through EXCHANGE_ID and CREATE_SESSION. Establishing a client identity also releases any locking state from a previous incarnation of that client. A client that wants delegations or other state needing callbacks must make sure a backchannel exists, using BIND_CONN_TO_SESSION if needed, and tells the server what callback security it accepts through BACKCHANNEL_CTL.

The client identifies itself with a client_owner4: a verifier that changes on each client restart and an owner string that stays the same across restarts. If the verifier differs from what the server recorded, the server starts cancelling the old leased state.
sections.plainLanguage: A session is like a library card kept on file. You can walk in through any door, and the librarian still knows who you are and what you borrowed.

sections.title: Exactly Once Semantics and the Reply Cache
sections.content:
Every COMPOUND that starts with a SEQUENCE operation MUST be executed exactly once. SEQUENCE MUST be the first operation and carries the session identifier plus the data needed for this guarantee. The RFC explains why even idempotent requests need it. A repeated RENAME gives a wrong error. A repeated WRITE can corrupt data, because a slow original can overwrite a later write that overlapped it after the retry has already been answered.

Old NFS duplicate caches keyed on the 32-bit RPC transaction ID (XID) and evicted entries by least recently used, so they were never perfect. NFSv4.1 instead uses a slot table. The requester picks an unused slot ID in the range 0 to N, where N starts as ca_maxrequests minus 1 and can be changed by SEQUENCE replies. Each slot holds a sequence ID and the cached reply for the request sent with it.

The sequence ID is a 32-bit unsigned value. The first use of a slot MUST use sequence ID one, and every reuse MUST be one greater than the last, wrapping from 0xFFFFFFFF to zero. If the number matches the cached one, the server returns the cached reply instead of running the request again. The number of outstanding requests is bounded by the slot table, so the cache has a bounded size and can be kept in persistent storage, though complete exactly once behavior is only possible when the server persists the reply cache and never needs to restart.
sections.plainLanguage: Each order gets a numbered ticket in a numbered slot. If you ask again with the same ticket, the cook hands back the meal already made instead of cooking a second one.

sections.title: State, Stateids and Leases
sections.content:
NFSv4 is stateful. When the server grants any lock, whether an open, a byte-range lock, a delegation or a layout, it returns a stateid, a 128-bit value that stands for that lock or set of locks. A stateid is always interpreted against the client ID of the current session, and it may be used on any session of the same client ID. Stateids come in these kinds: opens, sets of byte-range locks, file delegations, directory delegations and layouts. The seqid inside changes when the state changes.

All of a client's state shares one lease. Any request on a session, via a successful SEQUENCE on an unexpired lease, renews it for the period given by the lease_time attribute. If the client stops renewing, the server may release its locks once the lease expires, so other clients are not blocked forever by a crashed one. The lease is not a cache consistency mechanism.

If the server loses its state, for example after a restart, clients discover it through errors such as NFS4ERR_BADSESSION, NFS4ERR_DEADSESSION or NFS4ERR_STALE_CLIENTID. They then recreate a session or a new client ID and reclaim their locks using reclaim-type requests during a grace period; layouts are an exception because they are not reclaimed. The RECLAIM_COMPLETE operation tells the server a client has finished reclaiming.
sections.plainLanguage: A stateid is a coat-check ticket for something you hold. Your tickets all stay valid as long as you keep checking in. If you vanish, the shop eventually gives your things to someone else.

sections.title: Delegations and Client-Side Caching
sections.content:
A delegation lets the server hand a client the right to handle a file locally, so it avoids repeated requests while no other client conflicts. It is recallable: when another client conflicts, the server uses a callback to recall it. A server avoids delegating until it has found that a backchannel exists, and clients MUST NOT assume a delegation will be granted.

There are two kinds of open delegation. OPEN_DELEGATE_READ lets many clients read at once without conflict, and the holder is assured that contents and most attributes will not change without its knowledge. OPEN_DELEGATE_WRITE is exclusive, so the holder can modify data locally. A server can recall a delegation whenever it likes, and operations from other protocols or local access that would break the guarantee must also trigger a recall.

NFSv4.1 extends this. Delegations may now be held on non-regular files. WANT_DELEGATION lets a client ask for a delegation it was denied. GET_DIR_DELEGATION gives a read-only directory delegation covering the directory attributes and entries, which helps workloads with many lookups of names that do not exist, such as compiling software. A client can also ask for notifications of directory changes so it is not recalled each time.
sections.plainLanguage: The server lends you a file to work on at your own desk. If someone else needs it, the server calls and asks for it back.

sections.title: Parallel NFS (pNFS)
sections.content:
pNFS is an OPTIONAL feature. It splits file service in two: a metadata server handles names, attributes and permissions, while clients read and write file data straight to storage devices in parallel. The data path uses a storage protocol, which may be NFSv4.1 itself, a block protocol such as iSCSI, or an object protocol. Control between the metadata server and the storage devices is outside the scope of the RFC. A pNFS server MUST still support normal NFSv4.1 access to every file, so clients without a matching storage protocol keep working.

The key object is the layout, a recallable, leased and revocable object that maps a byte range of a file to storage devices. It belongs to a layout type that defines the storage protocol, and a client must hold a layout to do I/O to a storage device. The flow is: GETATTR for fs_layout_type, EXCHANGE_ID asking for EXCHGID4_FLAG_USE_PNFS_MDS, OPEN, LAYOUTGET, GETDEVICEINFO to find device addresses, I/O to the devices, and LAYOUTCOMMIT to report the new size and modification time.

The file layout type (LAYOUT4_NFSV4_1_FILES, Section 13) uses NFSv4.1 data servers and stripes data in units across them. A client may send them only housekeeping operations (such as EXCHANGE_ID, CREATE_SESSION and SEQUENCE) and the I/O operations COMMIT, READ, WRITE and PUTFH, always with the filehandle from the layout. Anything else gets NFS4ERR_NOTSUPP. A server's pNFS role comes from its EXCHANGE_ID flags: metadata server, data server or non-metadata server.
sections.plainLanguage: One clerk keeps the catalog and tells you which shelves hold your book pieces. Then you go to all those shelves at once and pick them up yourself, which is much faster.

sections.title: One Namespace Across Servers
sections.content:
A server presents all its exports as a single tree reachable from a per-server root filehandle, so a client can browse with LOOKUP and READDIR. Where parts of the path are not exported, the server fills the gap with a read-only pseudo file system. Each pseudo file system MUST have its own fsid, unique on that server. The RFC's example has /a as pseudo, /a/b as real, /a/b/c as pseudo and /a/b/c/d as real.

Across servers, location attributes (fs_locations, fs_locations_info) say where a file system lives. Combined with absent file systems, which have no content but specify locations, they provide referrals to other servers, replicas to use if one instance fails, and non-disruptive migration of a file system to another server.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole network looks like one big folder tree, even though the folders sit on different machines. Signs tell you when a folder has moved next door.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC calls the old model, in which the server trusts the client machine and uses AUTH_SYS, unsafe. Implementations are REQUIRED to support end-to-end authentication where a user mutually authenticates to a principal on the server. Users may decline integrity protection for speed, but that leaves a man-in-the-middle able to modify requests and replies.

Three cases deserve integrity protection regardless of user choice. SECINFO and SECINFO_NO_NAME are RECOMMENDED to be protected with an integrity-protecting flavor, since an attacker could otherwise push the client toward a weaker option. Any GETATTR for fs_locations or fs_locations_info SHOULD also use integrity protection, to stop an attacker faking NFS4ERR_MOVED and then redirecting the client to a hostile server.

NFSv4.1 adds further considerations for pNFS, locking and session state, state reclaim during the grace period, and the SSV-based RPCSEC_GSS mechanism. The impact of pNFS on security varies with the storage protocol and can be as low as zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone sitting between two computers could change the notes they pass. Signing each note and checking it keeps the sneaky middle person out.
